The heritage

One thread, four thousand years long.

دھاگا

Follow the line. Each knot in it marks a place where a craft took the shape you see in the aisle ahead.

c. 2500 BCE

Indus Valley, Sindh

Cloth that was already dyed

The cities of the Indus grew cotton and worked with dye. The carved Priest-King of Mohenjo-daro wears a shawl with a repeating trefoil pattern, and Sindhis often point to it as an ancestor of the Ajrak printed today in indigo and madder red.

11th–15th c.

Multan and Uch

Blue glaze comes up the river

Cobalt and turquoise tilework begins to cover the shrines of Multan and Uch Sharif. The word kashi is commonly traced to the tile makers of Kashan, and the craft survives as Multan blue pottery.

1556–1707

Mughal Lahore

The workshop becomes a court

Under the Mughals, Lahore holds a fort, gardens and a studio of painters. Wazir Khan Mosque is covered in tile and fresco, and the Badshahi Mosque is completed in 1673. Miniature painting learns to put a garden in the palm of a hand.

1700s–1900s

Punjab's villages and Chiniot

Hands that never stopped

Women in Punjab stitch phulkari for dowries and festivals, counting threads without a drawn pattern. In Chiniot, carpenters carve shisham wood into doors, screens and balconies for whole houses.

Mid-20th c. on

Karachi, Rawalpindi, Peshawar

The truck becomes a canvas

As trucks take over the roads, drivers hire painters to cover them in flowers, birds and verses. The art moves, and a new kind of gallery starts to cross the country every day.

The aisle

Six works, six pairs of hands

راہداری

Six crafts, one country

Made by hand, carried by families.

دستکاری

From painted trucks to hand-carved doors, here is a closer look at the crafts that give Pakistan its colour, and where each one lives.

Karachi · Rawalpindi · Peshawar · Lahore

Truck Art ٹرک آرٹ

Pakistan’s trucks, buses and rickshaws are painted like moving galleries. Artists cover every panel with flowers, birds, mountains, portraits and lines of poetry, then add shimmering chamak patti reflective strips, hanging chains and bells. A single vehicle can take days or weeks to finish, and the colour is meant to turn a long road into a celebration.

  • Enamel paint
  • Chamak patti
  • Poetry panels

Lahore · Karachi · Across the Urdu world

Calligraphy خطاطی

Khattati is treated as the noblest of the visual arts. Urdu is written mostly in Nastaliq, a flowing, slanting script that seems to hang from an invisible line. The calligrapher cuts a reed pen, the qalam, and practises for years before a line looks effortless. In Lahore you can read it in the tile and fresco inscriptions of Wazir Khan Mosque, and Sadequain (1930–1987) carried it onto gallery walls and murals.

  • Nastaliq
  • Reed qalam
  • Sadequain

Punjab · Sindh · Balochistan · Swat

Embroidery کڑھائی

Every region stitches differently. Punjab’s phulkari, “flower work”, covers shawls in silk floss darning stitches; Sindh is known for mirror-work and dense geometric kashida; Balochistan for heavy, richly coloured stitching on dresses; and Swat and Kohistan for bright floral panels. Gold-thread zardozi is still worked by hand in the workshops of Lahore and Karachi for bridal and festive wear.

  • Phulkari
  • Mirror-work
  • Zardozi

Sindh · Balochistan · Punjab · Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Basketry ٹوکری سازی

Baskets, mats and fans are woven from whatever grows nearby. In Sindh and Balochistan, women split the leaves of the mazri (dwarf palm) and plait them into mats, baskets and bread holders. In Punjab, sarkanda reed and munj grass become sieves, stools and the rope strung across a charpai, while bamboo and cane are woven in the north. These cheap, strong objects are now being replaced by plastic.

  • Mazri palm
  • Munj grass
  • Cane & bamboo

Chiniot · Swat · Kohistan · Old Lahore

Wood Carving لکڑی کی نقاشی

Chiniot, in Punjab, is the country’s best-known centre of woodcarving. Craftsmen work shisham (Indian rosewood) and other hardwoods into doors, jharokas (balconies), screens, chairs and chests, carving deep floral and geometric relief and often inlaying brass or bone. Swat and Kohistan are known for carved deodar pillars and house fronts, and the old city of Lahore still keeps carved balconies and doors on its streets.

  • Shisham
  • Jali screens
  • Brass inlay

Sindh · Multan · Bahawalpur · Faisalabad

Fabrics & Textiles کپڑا اور ٹیکسٹائل

Cloth is Pakistan’s oldest craft and its biggest industry. Sindh prints ajrak with resist dyes and wooden blocks in indigo and madder red; Multan and Bahawalpur weave khes and susi; Sindhi rilli quilts stitch scraps into patchwork; and Faisalabad, nicknamed the “Manchester of Pakistan”, is a major mill city. Cotton, lawn, khaddar and silk travel from village looms to mills to wardrobes around the world.

  • Ajrak
  • Khes & susi
  • Rilli quilts

Voices of the land

Pakistan’s poets and writers.

شاعر و ادیب

The pen has been as busy as the loom. Verses are stitched on shawls and painted across the tail boards of trucks, and these are some of the voices behind them.

Poetsشعرا

I

Allama Muhammad Iqbal

علامہ محمد اقبال

1877–1938 · Sialkot · Lahore

The “Poet of the East” and the thinker most closely linked with the idea of Pakistan. He wrote in Urdu and Persian, and his Allahabad address of 1930 shaped the case for a separate homeland. His tomb stands beside the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore.

Read: Bang-e-Dra · Asrar-e-Khudi · Bal-e-Jibril

F

Faiz Ahmed Faiz

فیض احمد فیض

1911–1984 · Sialkot district · Lahore

The poet of love and resistance. Jailed in the early 1950s, he wrote some of his finest verse in prison. “Hum Dekhenge” became an anthem of protest, and he received the Lenin Peace Prize.

Read: Naqsh-e-Faryadi · Dast-e-Saba · Zindan Nama

A

Ahmad Faraz

احمد فراز

1931–2008 · Kohat · Islamabad

A modern Urdu ghazal poet loved for romantic verse and outspoken protest. His ghazal “Ranjish Hi Sahi” was sung by Mehdi Hassan and remains a classic. In 2006 he returned a national honour to protest against the government.

Read: Ranjish Hi Sahi · Dard Aashob

P

Parveen Shakir

پروین شاکر

1952–1994 · Karachi · Islamabad

She gave Urdu poetry a fresh, confident feminine voice. Her first book, Khushbu (1976), made her famous in her twenties. She died in a road accident in Islamabad at the age of 42.

Read: Khushbu · Sad-barg · Inkaar

J

Habib Jalib

حبیب جالب

1928–1993 · Hoshiarpur · Lahore

The people’s poet. His poem “Dastoor” challenged military rule, and he went to jail more than once for what he recited. He is remembered for plain, fearless verse that crowds could chant.

Read: Dastoor · Mein Nahin Manta

B

Bulleh Shah

بلھے شاہ

c. 1680–1757 · Punjab · Kasur

A Sufi poet of Punjabi kafis who questioned empty ritual and preached love and tolerance. His verses are still sung by qawwals and folk singers, and his shrine in Kasur draws visitors all year.

Read: Kafis · Bulleh Nu Samjhavan

W

Waris Shah

وارث شاہ

1722–1798 · Punjab

He wrote the best-loved telling of the love story of Heer and Ranjha in Punjabi, composed in 1766. It is widely regarded as a classic of Punjabi literature, and its lines are quoted at village gatherings to this day.

Read: Heer Waris Shah

S

Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai

شاہ عبداللطیف بھٹائی

1689–1752 · Sindh · Bhit Shah

Sindh’s great Sufi poet. His Shah Jo Risalo retells folk tales of heroines such as Sassui, Marui and Sohni, and is sung by musicians at his shrine at Bhit Shah.

Read: Shah Jo Risalo

Writersادیب

M

Saadat Hasan Manto

سعادت حسن منٹو

1912–1955 · Samrala · Lahore

The master of the Urdu short story. He wrote unflinchingly about Partition and the lives of people on the margins, faced obscenity trials for it, and died in Lahore at 42.

Read: Toba Tek Singh · Khol Do · Thanda Gosht

B

Bano Qudsia

بانو قدسیہ

1928–2017 · Firozpur · Lahore

Novelist, playwright and television writer. Her novel Raja Gidh (1981) is one of the most widely read and discussed Urdu novels of its time.

Read: Raja Gidh · Aadhi Baat

A

Ashfaq Ahmed

اشفاق احمد

1925–2004 · Punjab · Lahore

A storyteller for radio, television and the page, best known for his Zavia talks and plays that mix everyday life with questions about faith and meaning.

Read: Zavia · Gadaria · Talqeen Shah

I

Intizar Hussain

انتظار حسین

1923–2016 · Dibai · Lahore

A fiction writer who drew on myth, memory and the loss of Partition. He settled in Lahore in 1947, and his novel Basti is a landmark; he was shortlisted for the Man Booker International Prize in 2013.

Read: Basti · Agle Zamane Ki Kahaniyan

B

Bapsi Sidhwa

بپسی سدھوا

1938–2024 · Karachi · Lahore

A Parsi novelist who grew up in Lahore. Her novel Ice-Candy Man (published in the US as Cracking India) tells the story of Partition through a child’s eyes and inspired the film Earth.

Read: Ice-Candy Man · The Crow Eaters

M

Mohsin Hamid

محسن حامد

b. 1971 · Lahore

A Lahore-born novelist read around the world. The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2007) was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, and Exit West followed in 2017.

Read: The Reluctant Fundamentalist · Exit West

Voices of the land

Pakistan’s singers and sound.

گلوکار اور موسیقار

Poetry travels furthest when it is sung. From the qawwali of the shrines to the ghazal of the concert hall and the folk songs of the villages, these voices carried the verses of Pakistan’s poets to the world.

Qawwaliقوالی

N

Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan

نصرت فتح علی خان

1948–1997 · Faisalabad

Known as “Shahenshah-e-Qawwali”, the king of kings of qawwali. He came from a family of qawwals and took the devotional form to concert halls around the world, working with artists such as Peter Gabriel and Eddie Vedder. His voice could stretch one line into a half-hour of rising ecstasy.

Listen: Mera Piya Ghar Aaya · Allah Hoo · Tumhein Dillagi

S

The Sabri Brothers

صابری برادران

Ghulam Farid (1930–1994) & Maqbool (1945–2011) · Karachi

Among the most celebrated qawwali ensembles of the twentieth century, led by the brothers Ghulam Farid and Maqbool Sabri. They carried the Sufi devotional tradition to audiences abroad, including a performance at Carnegie Hall in 1975. Ghulam Farid’s son Amjad Sabri continued the family art until his death in 2016.

Listen: Bhar Do Jholi Meri · Tajdar-e-Haram

A

Aziz Mian

عزیز میاں

1942–2000 · Delhi · Lahore

A qawwal of raw power and philosophical bite. He broke up his songs with long spoken passages, arguing with God, love and the world, and his “Main Sharabi” remains one of the best-known qawwalis of its kind.

Listen: Main Sharabi · Hashr Ke Roz

R

Rahat Fateh Ali Khan

راحت فتح علی خان

b. 1973 · Faisalabad

Nephew and student of Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. He grew up on the stage with his uncle and became one of South Asia’s best-known voices, moving easily between qawwali, Coke Studio and film songs.

Listen: Zaroori Tha · Teri Ore · Jag Soona Soona Lage

Ghazal and classicalغزل

M

Mehdi Hassan

مہدی حسن

1927–2012 · Rajasthan · Karachi

Called “Shahenshah-e-Ghazal”, the emperor of the ghazal. He came from a long line of hereditary musicians, and his slow, patient delivery made the poems of Ghalib, Faiz and Faraz feel newly spoken.

Listen: Ranjish Hi Sahi · Zindagi Mein To Sabhi Pyar Kiya Karte Hain

N

Noor Jehan

نور جہاں

1926–2000 · Kasur · Karachi

“Malika-e-Tarannum”, the queen of melody. She began as a child singer in Punjab, became a star actress, and after 1947 sang for Pakistani films for decades in Urdu and Punjabi, leaving behind thousands of songs.

Listen: Awaz De Kahan Hai · Chandni Raatein · Mauja Hi Mauja

I

Iqbal Bano

اقبال بانو

1935–2009 · Delhi · Lahore

A ghazal and semi-classical singer whose name is tied to Faiz’s poem “Hum Dekhenge”. In 1985 she sang it before a huge Lahore crowd, wearing a black sari at a time when the dictatorship discouraged it, and the recording became a symbol of resistance.

Listen: Hum Dekhenge · Dasht-e-Tanhai

F

Farida Khanum

فریدہ خانم

1929–2014 · Amritsar · Lahore

Known as “Malika-e-Ghazal”. Trained in the classical tradition, she was admired for a restrained, grave style, and for the way she sang a poem so that every word was heard.

Listen: Aaj Jane Ki Zid Na Karo · Woh Mujh Se Hue Hamkalaam

Folk and Sufiلوک و صوفی

A

Abida Parveen

عابدہ پروین

b. 1954 · Larkana

Often called the queen of Sufi music. She sings kafi, ghazal and qawwali with a voice that moves from a whisper to a cry, and her settings of Bulleh Shah and Shah Latif have reached listeners in Pakistan and abroad.

Listen: Tere Ishq Nachaya · Yaar Ko Hum Ne · Ranjha Ranjha

R

Reshma

ریشماں

c. 1947–2013 · Rajasthan · Karachi

A folk singer with a deep, earthy voice, born into a nomadic family. Her song of separation, “Lambi Judai”, was heard on both sides of the border, and she sang for decades in Punjabi, Sindhi and Rajasthani styles.

Listen: Lambi Judai · Wey Main Chori Chori

A

Alam Lohar

عالم لوہار

1928–1979 · Punjab

The great voice of Punjabi folk storytelling. He sang the old tales of Heer, Sassui and Saif-ul-Malook to the beat of his chimta, an iron tong, and his “Jugni” is still sung in Punjab.

Listen: Jugni · Saif-ul-Malook

A

Allan Fakir

الن فقیر

1932–2000 · Sindh

A Sindhi folk and Sufi singer who sang the verses of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai and Sachal Sarmast in a fervent, spinning style. He drew crowds at shrines and festivals across Sindh.

Listen: Kalam of Shah Latif · Sufi kafis

Pop and rockپاپ و راک

N

Nazia Hassan

نازیہ حسن

1965–2000 · Karachi

The teenage voice behind “Aap Jaisa Koi” (1980). She became the first Pakistani to win a Filmfare Award, and with her brother Zoheb she made South Asian pop that young people could dance to. She died of cancer at 35.

Listen: Aap Jaisa Koi · Disco Deewane · Boom Boom

J

Junoon

جنون

Formed 1990 · Lahore

A band that fused rock guitar with Sufi poetry, led by Salman Ahmad and Ali Azmat. They set verses of Bulleh Shah and Iqbal to a rock beat and became one of Pakistan’s best-loved bands.

Listen: Sayonee · Jazba-e-Junoon · Bulleya

Eyes of the land

Pakistan’s painters and artists.

مصور اور فنکار

The same hands that paint a truck or stitch a shawl have also filled galleries. These artists took miniature, calligraphy and modern painting into new territory.

Masters and pioneersاساتذہ

S

Sadequain

صادقین

1930–1987 · Amroha · Karachi

The best-known name in Pakistani calligraphic painting. He turned Quranic verses and Urdu poetry into sweeping murals, among them the ceiling of Frere Hall in Karachi, and he illustrated the verses of Ghalib.

Look: Treasures of Time (Mangla Dam) · Frere Hall murals

A

Abdur Rahman Chughtai

عبدالرحمٰن چغتائی

1894–1975 · Lahore

A Lahore painter who blended Mughal miniature and Persian line with the Bengal school. His romantic, long-limbed figures illustrated the verses of Ghalib and Iqbal, and he is counted among the founders of modern painting in the subcontinent.

Look: Muraqqa-e-Chughtai · Mughal-style watercolours

G

Ismail Gulgee

اسماعیل گل جی

1926–2007 · Peshawar

An abstract painter famous for calligraphic canvases and for his mirror-mosaic work, which breaks light into hundreds of tiny reflecting pieces. He brought Islamic script into the language of modern abstraction.

Look: Calligraphic abstracts · Mirror-mosaic panels

Z

Zubeida Agha

زبیدہ آغا

1922–1997

Widely regarded as a pioneer of modern abstract painting in Pakistan. Her early works in the 1940s and 1950s broke away from realism and opened the way for a generation of younger painters.

Look: Early abstract canvases

S

Shakir Ali

شاکر علی

1916–1975 · Rampur · Lahore

A painter and teacher whose cubist-influenced work mixed European modernism with local forms. As principal of the National College of Arts in Lahore he shaped many of the country’s later artists.

Look: Still lifes · Cubist figure studies

A

Anna Molka Ahmed

انا مولکا احمد

1917–1994 · England · Lahore

Born in England, she settled in Lahore and founded the Fine Arts Department at the University of the Punjab. She was a painter and a teacher, and generations of Pakistani artists studied under her.

Look: Portraits and figure paintings

J

Jamil Naqsh

جمیل نقش

1939–2019 · Kairana · Karachi

A figurative painter known for his stylised women and his pigeons, in warm reds and golds. His flowing lines drew on Mughal miniature and modern painting alike.

Look: Women and pigeon series

Contemporary artistsمعاصر فنکار

S

Salima Hashmi

سلیمہ ہاشمی

b. 1942 · Lahore

Artist, teacher and curator, and the daughter of the poet Faiz Ahmed Faiz. She taught for decades at the National College of Arts, later served as its principal, and helped bring Pakistani art to wider attention.

Look: Paintings · Exhibitions she curated

S

Shazia Sikander

شازیہ سکندر

b. 1969 · Lahore

Trained in miniature painting at the National College of Arts in Lahore, she stretches the old form into large-scale drawing, animation and installation. She received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2006.

Look: Miniature-based works · Video animations

R

Rashid Rana

رشید رانا

b. 1968 · Lahore

A conceptual artist who builds large images out of thousands of tiny photographs, so that a picture changes completely as you step closer. His work asks how images, places and identities are put together.

Look: Photo-mosaic works

I

Imran Qureshi

عمران قریشی

b. 1972 · Hyderabad, Sindh · Lahore

Trained in miniature painting, he is known for delicate floral patterns and for red paint poured over floors and walls. His roof-garden commission at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 2013 made him known worldwide.

Look: Roof Garden Commission (2013) · Miniature paintings

Why it matters

Secondary research.

ثانوی تحقیق

Start with the world, come home to Pakistan, walk the streets of Lahore, then ask why a craft fades and what is lost when it does.

Global perspective National perspective Local perspective · Lahore Causes & consequences

Perspective 01

Global Perspectives

عالمی نقطۂ نظر

3.1%of global GDP comes from creative and traditional industries (UNCTAD, Creative Economy Outlook 2022)
6.2%of total employment worldwide (UNCTAD, Creative Economy Outlook 2022)
75.6%of global creative goods exports in 2022 were crafts and design products. The figure includes design goods, not only traditional handicrafts (UNCTAD, 2024)

Internationally, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) identifies those traditional arts and crafts are crucial segment in intangible cultural heritage. They restore the beliefs, skills and customs delivered from generation to generations. UNESCO highlights to protect cultural heritage for assuring its existence in our societies. This tells that the decrease of arts and crafts is a major challenge for protection of different cultures and their identities. Yet without it the identity and name that a culture stands might be lost over time if the artistic mastery and traditional guidance is not passed down (UNESCO, 2003). Overall, resembling the significance of sustaining and honouring the diversification of various cultures for upcoming generations.

Likewise, the UNCTAD recognizes that innovative industries flourish economic development by giving employment opportunities and aiding local businesses. In accordance to UNTAD’s Creative Economy Outlook 2022, it is estimated that visionary and traditional industries allocated for 3.1% of global GDP and 6.2% of total employment. This infers to the declining pursuits in cultural craftsmanship, indicating a negative impact on artisans of less employment opportunities, incomes and turning down of local economies. Inadequate financial support, increased demand for mass-produced products and different views of customers are the leading factors behind the decline of arts & crafts. As a result, skilled and hardworking labour will turn down their jobs, weakening the cultural identity of the area (UN, 2022).

Further, UNESCO accentuate the significance of teaching and passing customs, traditions and skills among generations. Due to lack of interest among youth in learning traditional artistry, crafts, important methodologies and cultural values creates the danger of disappearance of traditional arts and crafts. The long-term consequences stretch beyond cultural loss, as many destinations will be left out of tourism opportunities and fewer employment seekers (UNESCO, Safeguarding strategy of traditional crafts for peace building, 2019). This highlights the urgent need of safeguarding craftsmanship, not just for maintenance of cultural integrity but also protecting a profession that has skills passed by various generations. It is also a step for developing sustainable livelihoods.

Furthermore, UNCTAD’s Creative Economy Outlook 2024 suggests that crafts and design products shared 75.6% of global creative goods exports in 2022. This emphasizes the notable global markets for innovative goods, although the value includes creative products largely than traditional handicrafts only. It tells that custom and cultural craftmanship can gain its economic depth when artists would have the assistance and access to markets (UN, Creative Economy Outlook 2024, 2024).

Perspective 02

National Perspective

قومی نقطۂ نظر

The meaning of art and crafts in todays culture has descended in popularity and especially in Pakistan, as people think that because of modern tools and the effect of society has played a pivotal role in the decline of arts and crafts. The crafts that are made by these people contain a hidden story, they are pieces of art which are fading away. Some reasons why arts and crafts are significantly declining in society is that it is very labour intensive. According to Dawn news, the remaining arjak makers spend more than 10 hours producing two pieces of cloth, and what they earn is not even enough to provide for themselves and their family. The prices of raw materials has increased rapidly in the past years which make it even more difficult for arjak makers to produce fabric easily (Dawn, 2010).

These factors have caused for people to discontinue their passion. As in this current state of the world art has lost its relevance and in a world where machinery can be made for very little money, alternatives like these have taken over. Traditional arts such as: Embroidery, hand-tooled leatherwork, woodcarving and handcrafted musical instruments are becoming obsolete because of the lack of support from the government. The Peshawari chappals were in a time the type of sandal in which the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa felt pride in the making of it but as of today the production of them has decreased as factory versions are cheaper and faster to make (Rana, 2025).

Artisans in Pakistan face numerous challenges like poor infrastructure, lack of access to mainstream markets and being used by middlemen. Foreign influence has also posed a threat to Pakistani culture. The consequences for this downfall are that losing regional crafts like Multan’s blue pottery and Balochistan’s embroidery cuts the line between historical roots. Hereditary skills and ancient techniques for craftsmanship vanish because of the younger generation as they migrate to cities instead of learning manual trades (Naeem, 2012).

Tribal women who make these crafts lose economic recognition due to a lack of fair market access. The reason why protecting and supporting this perspective is important because the culture of arts and crafts is deteriorating and to fix this problem we need the government’s help. This is necessary as they can introduce a system of subsidies and state support made for the promotion of traditional arts, crafts and professions. We could have big brands partner with artisans to bring their work to the big stage (Zafar, 2024).

A lot of initiatives have taken place to preserve the historical importance of arts and crafts in Pakistan. According to the article Arts and Crafts in Pakistan by Mehrdad Rakhshandeh, where non-governmental organizations provide training and economic support to promote handicraft traditions. Traditional products of Pakistan are up for showcasing at exhibitions and museums. However, the article highlights insufficient support for younger generations as a still going challenge (Rakhshandeh, 2026).

Art has also declined in Lahore where at first it used to be lively, filled with emotions and feeling, these pieces of articulate craftmanship allowed artisans to express their true thoughts.

Perspective 03

Local Perspective: Lahore

لاہور

It has been a way to entertain; it was practiced by individuals who mastered the way to express their feelings and emotions that cannot be replicated by just regular pictures. Some Pakistani art staples where at Lahore – truck art brings bright colors with precise steel cutting has transformed normal trucks into moving artwork. Cultural brass and copperware such as beaten trays, vases and lanterns are the cultural identity of Pakistan. The sight of traditional ceramics, tile making and blue pottery can be seen on monuments like the Lahore fort and Wazir Khan Mosque. Lahori woodwork can also be seen in traditional architecture and furniture. But these fine works of art are disappearing before our very eyes (harryjohnstone, 2019).

According to research it shows that the decrease in popularity is due to the mass production and use of machinery today. This has led to major harm in the world of arts and crafts. Loss of ancestral patronage and younger generations steering away from artisanal traditions. Some consequences that occur because of these causes are the loss of authentic historical skills and the loss of ancient techniques to make these masterpieces. There could also be the loss of small-scale family-owned businesses. Displacement of materials and goods like hand loomed textiles and hand beaten metalwork and pottery and being replaced by plastic and synthetic goods.

According to finds today solutions to this issue are being done as the government of Punjab has launched a master plan to transform and modernize the Lahore Arts Council. This plan aims to support artists and hold exhibitions such as the Museum Collection Conservation & Re-framing Project to further help art retain its identity in Lahore (Ali, 2015).

The Lahore pictures are illustrations painted in code.

Secondary research

Causes and Consequences

اسباب اور نتائج

Causes

A primary driver behind the marginalization of traditional arts and crafts is the rise of modernization. The modern world has become simpler, from beautiful colors to just shades of grey and white. This is due to the cheaper manufacturing and efficient production of simpler designs. “Machine-made imitations are everywhere, sold for less and made in a fraction of the time.” (Rana, 2025) Because factories prioritize low production costs and high output to manage consumer demand, time intensive local crafts that feature intricate patterns and specialized hand techniques are increasingly pushed out of the market. Ultimately, speed and affordability are valued over the authenticity of handmade goods.

In addition to modernization, the lack of recognition and low wages of traditional craftsmanship prevent new generations from pursuing it as a career. The lack of financial stability and security are the primary challenges faced by artists in Pakistan. (Ahmed, 2025) Despite the immense skill and time required to master these techniques, most people often rank manual labor below modern, formal occupations. Furthermore, consumers expect low market prices so middle agents and mass markets frequently underpay artisans, making their income unsustainable. Facing financial insecurity and minimal social prestige, younger individuals naturally seek employment in modern sectors instead, leaving local craft traditions with a shrinking workforce and no successors to carry them forward.

A crucial cause behind the decline of traditional crafts is the erosion of the Ustad-Shagird system. Complex crafting knowledge was not taught in formal institutions, but transmitted verbally and practically across generations. As access to formal modern education expands, younger generations prioritize city jobs. “Many young people regard such occupations as financially insecure and lacking social prestige.” (Soomro, 2026) Modern corporate occupations offer fixed, well paying salaries and higher respect in society, which artisan work fails to provide. Consequently, this informal way of passing down skills is breaking down quickly. Without young people willing to spend years learning from master craftspeople for low pay, ancient skills like detailed tilework and local embroidery will be lost forever.

Consequences

The current decline of handicraft sector increases the rate of rural unemployment and severe income instability across vulnerable cottage industries. In many provinces, small scale artisan workshops used to serve as primary income generators for agricultural households, boosting seasonal farming incomes. However, as demand for handmade goods decreases, rural craftspeople face prolonged periods of unemployment and significant wage drops. Consequently, artisan families are forced to rely on middle agents who keep most of the financial earnings. Additionally, cottage scale workshops are gradually shutting down, stripping thousands of workers of their primary source of income. This widespread loss of income severely diminishes purchasing power, worsening rural poverty. “Pakistan’s annual earnings from handicraft exports are estimated to be a mere few hundred million dollars, a fraction of the billions achieved by regional peers like India and Bangladesh.” (Ahmed S. H., 2026)

The decline of traditional craftsmanship significantly accelerates a global shift away from sustainable manufacturing processes. Historically, crafts relied almost entirely on locally sourced, biodegradable materials which include natural clays, plant-based dyes, organic cotton and ethically harvested timber. “Man has made colors synthetically which are used in different industries world-wide, causing damage to life and environment.” (Extraction and Application of Natural Pigments from Plant Sources as Sustainable Alternatives to Synthetic Dyes, 2025) These production methods created minimal waste. However, as these industries collapse under market pressure, consumers and manufacturers have started to rely on cheap, mass-produced artificial alternatives. Synthetic fabrics, plastic homeware, and chemical dyes generate toxic non-biodegradable waste, heavily polluting water and soil. Consequently, the erosion of traditional crafts not only threatens cultural heritage but also undermines critical efforts toward sustainable resource management and environmental preservation in rural communities.

Alongside the use of synthetic materials, the decline of traditional crafts results in the permanent loss of vital environmental knowledge. For generations, artisans held a deep understanding of local plants, seasonal harvesting times, and natural conservation methods. Master craftspeople understood how to extract plant dyes, harvest timber, and collect organic raw materials. This local environmental wisdom was transmitted through generations along with technical crafting skills. “Across Pakistan, many of these traditions are becoming fragile. When a craft disappears, Pakistan does not only lose an art form. It loses a memory.” (Noreen, 2026) As younger generations abandon traditional trades due to economic instability, this specialized environmental understanding is rapidly disappearing. Without documentation or active practice, centuries of sustainable resource preservation are permanently erased, leaving rural areas more vulnerable to environmental damage and the impacts of climate change.

The most important cause and consequence

We believe that rapid modernization and the expansion of industrialization serve as the main causes behind the decline of traditional craft industries. Modern markets highly favor mass production, shifting consumer preferences toward simplified aesthetics that rely on neutral tones and uniform designs. Industrial facilities use automated machinery and artificial raw materials to produce huge quantities of goods at a speed and cost that small scale cottage industries cannot compete with. Factory-made alternatives offer consumers inexpensive copies of traditional products. Because industrial manufacturers prioritize low cost and high output rates, labor intensive cottage industries, which depend on fine handcrafting methods, natural dyes, and extended production cycles, are progressively pushed to the margins of the economy. Consequently, contemporary market dynamics value rapid turnaround times and low prices over the structural quality, cultural significance, and authenticity in handmade goods. “With the increasing influence of modernization and industrialization, these traditional crafts are at risk of being lost.” (Desk, 2024)

As a result, the issues have caused a significant shift from ecologically sustainable manufacturing models toward environmentally damaging industrial processes. Historically, cottage industry manufacturing relied mainly on naturally produced, biodegradable inputs, such as organic fibers, plant based pigments, unrefined clays, and responsibly harvested timber which generated minimal industrial output waste. “As the textile industry continues to prioritize sustainability, natural dyes offer a compelling alternative to synthetic dyes.” (Leo Marcom Pvt Ltd, n.d.) However, as local cottage industries give way to commercial pressure, market demand has transitioned toward petroleum-based synthetic fabrics, plastic goods, and toxic chemical dyes. The widespread manufacturing and disposal of these artificial alternatives generate non-biodegradable waste that contaminates surrounding soil and water ecosystems.
